newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: Uzbekistan courts foreign oil and gas investors.
newsitem.headline: Uzbekistan courts foreign oil and gas investors.

text.p: Uzbekistan plans to overhaul its key oil and gas sector with the help of Western partners and increased fuel efficiency, the chairman of state oil and gas concern Uzbekneftegaz said on Thursday.

At the first major oil and gas conference in Tashkent since the Central Asian republic's independence from Moscow in 1991, senior Uzbek officials and potential Western partners expressed a desire to work together.
"In order to actively attract foreign partners in the development of the country's economic sectors, the government has created a favourable legal basis," Uzbekneftegaz Chairman Kayim Khakkulov said.
He said Tahskent had made the energy industry a priority among the myriad of valuable raw material sectors which bless the former Soviet republic.
Uzbekistan has not yet attracted the foreign investment dollars its energy-rich neighbours -- Russia, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan -- have. But deals are in the works.

Khudaykul Zhumayev, a deputy chairman of Uzbekneftegaz, said the firm was in talks with several big Western oil firms, including Mobil Corp and Unocal of the United States, Delta Oil of Saudi Arabia and Agip SpA of Italy.
The talks were of an open nature and included the possibility of working with foreign firms in joint ventures and on production-sharing agreements.

The Central Asian republic of 23 million has already completed several deals with foreign firms to upgrade oil refineries, and has a major $1.2 billion gas deal in the pipeline with Enron Oil & Gas Co of the United States.
Gas produced from the venture is expected to move to European markets via Russian natural gas monopoly Gazprom's GAZP.RTS sprawling pipeline system.
The project will produce around six billion cubic metres, or bcms, of natural gas annually, a level sustainable for up to 50 years, Zaynutdinov said.

According to Uzbekneftegaz estimates, Uzbek hydrocarbon reserves comprise 4.4 billion tonnes of oil, 629 million tonnes of gas condensate and 5.429 trillion cubic metres of gas. The country is also rich in gold, copper, zinc, uranium and molybdenum.
Future cooperation with foreign companies could include oil and oil-product swaps with Western firms, according to Jan Kalicki, Counselor to the United States Department of Commerce.
Uzbekistan expects to produce 8.0 million tonnes of oil and gas condensates in 1997, up from 7.66 million in 1996.
It wants to boost output further to 10.0 million tonnes by 2000, allowing exports of around two million tonnes annually.
Unlike some of its Central Asian neighbours, the mostly desert nation succeeded in boosting oil output sharply during the years following its independence from Moscow in 1991.
Gas output has also remained stable during the 1990s, reaching around 50 bcm last year, of which just over nine bcm was exported.
Now Uzbekistan is turning its attention towards fuel consumption as well as production.
Khakkulov said industrial energy consumers were so inefficient that proper use could cut offtake by 40 percent.
"The plan is to have savings of 10 bcm of natural gas annually by 2010, and I believe this will become a reality," he said.
